GUIDELINES FOR GRADING OF 
HIDES AND SKINS ON THE 
BASIS OF MASS AND SIZE

BUREAU OF INDIAN STANUABDS 
MANAK. IJHAVAN, V JJAHADUR SliAH ZAFAft MARG 

NEW DELHI 110W2 



e, I *l«» 19*5^ 



IS : 12435 - 1988 



Indian Standard 

GUIDELINES FOR GRADING OF 
HIDES AND SKINS ON THE 
BASIS OF MASS AND SIZE 

0. FOREWORD 



0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the 
Bureau of Indian Standards on 16 May 1988, 
after the draft finalized by the Leather Sectional 
Committee had been approved by the Chemical 
Division Council. 

0.2 Hides and skins are the basic raw materials 
for the leather industry and the cost of the finished 
leather is largely dependent on the cost of the raw 
hides, on their quality, mass, area and the types 
of leathers produced from them. 

0.3 It is recognized that raw hides and skins can 
be converted into different types of leather poss- 
essing certain special characteristics and used 
for various end uses. For example, calfskins are 
needed for producing quality shoe upper leather, 
heavier cow hides for boot upper, spready cow 
hides for upholstery leather and ox/buffalo hides 
for industrial leathers. Because of such specific 
requirements, hides and skins are graded through- 
out the world on the basis of mass and size 
besides other classification criteria — for example, 
quality, cure, animal breed and the source of 
origin. In India, cow and buffalo hides, and the 
skins of their calves are graded into different 
categories depending on their mass; and goat and 
sheep skins on the basis of area (generally the 
length). Though certain amount of uniformity 



exists in the classification of goat and sheep skins, 
no uniform method of classification of hides on 
mass basis exists in India today. Such classification 
vary from one raw hide dealer to other or from 
tanner to tanner. Considering the requests from 
the tanning industry to develop a uniform method 
of classification, the Leather Sectional Committee 
decided to formulate this Indian Standard. It is 
expected that this guideline will be beneficial to 
the tanners in having more uniformity in classi- 
fying hides and skins in India leaving certain 
detailed characteristics for agreement between the 
supplier and the purchaser. 

0.4 In the preparation of this standard, consi- 
derable assistance has been derived from the 
following publications: 

a) Report on the marketing of hides in India 
1967, Directorate of Marketing and Inspec- 
tion, Ministry of Food & Agriculture, 
Community Development & Cooperation, 
Government of India. 

b) Report on the Marketing of Skins in India 
( Revised Edition ), 1 955, Directorate of 
Marketing and Inspection, Ministry of 
Food and Agriculture, Government of 
India. 



1. SCOPE 

1,1 This standard prescribes guidelines for grading 
cow and buffalo calf skins, and buffalo hides on 
the basis of mass; and goat and sheep skins on 
the basis of length along the backbone line. 

2. TERMINOLOGY 

2.1 For the purpose of this guideline, the defini- 
tions given in IS: 1640-1960* shall apply. 

3. FLAYING, CURING AND PRESERVATION 
OF HIDES AND SKINS 

3,1 The cow and buffalo hides, and their calf 
skins; and goat and sheep skins shall be flayed. 



cured and preserved in accordance with IS:9663- 
1980* and IS:7656-l975t respectively. The hides 
and skins thus preserved shall have a moisture 
content in the range 40 to 50 percent when 
determined in accordance with A-4 of IS: 5570- 
1987J. 

4. GRADING OF COW AND BUFFALO CALF 
SKINS AND HIDES ON THE BASIS OF 
MASS 

4.1 In India, cow and buffalo hides include the 
hides of both female and castrated male. Bull 
hides are rarely available. Similarly calf skins 
also include the skins of both the male and 
female calves. 



♦Glossary of terms relating to hides, skins and leather. 



*Code of practice for flaying of hides and skins, 
fCode of practice for curing and preservation of cattle 
hides and goat and sheep skins by wet sahing method, 
{Specification for pickled goat skins {first revision ). 



1 



IS : 12435 - 1988 



4.2 Cow and buffalo hides and the calf skins are 
available in India today mostly in wet salted 
condition. A very small percentage of the hides 
are available in some remote areas either in dry 
salted or in dried stage. Such dry salted or dry 
hides are not generally used as the regular source 
of raw material for the commercial tanning 
centres in India. Similarly no green or fresh hide 
is available to the tanners for processing. In other 
countries, hides and calf skins are obtained as 
slaughter house by-products and the green weight 
is taken either in the slaughter house or by the 
raw hide dealers after procurement. In India, 
more than 80 percent of cattle hides are obtained 
from fallen animals scattered throughout the 
countryside and it is impracticable to record the 
green weight of the hides ofthe primary producers. 
It is thus apparent that classification of the wet 
salted hides and skins will meet the requirements 
of the Indian tanners. 

4.3 Determination of the Mass of Salted 
Hide/Skin 

4.3.1 Procedure — Each hide/skin of the batch 
to be checked is opened out, shaken violently by 
knocking it flesh side down against the ground or 
on a rectangular horse (40 cm in height). The 
remaining salt is removed by brushing. The hides 
are then weighed individually in order to deter- 
mine the category. The hide should be free from 
extraneous fat and flesh. The hide should be 
trimmed as prescribed in IS : 9160-1979*. The 
mass of each hide is expressed to the nearest 
0-5 kg. 

4.4 Classification — Cow and buff'alo hides and 
their calf skins are classified on the basis of mass 
as shown in Table 1. 

5. GRADING OF GOAT AND SHEEP SKINS 
ON THE BASIS OF LENGTH ALONG THE 
BACKBONE LINE 

5.1 Goat and sheep skins are generally available 
in India in wet salted condition only. 

5.2 Procedure for Measurement of the Length of 

the Skin — The skin having been folded length- 



wise and laid flat, the length along the backbone 
is to be measured from the root of the tail to the 
point where the skin of the front part of throat is 
the widest when determined at right angles to the 
fold. A diagrammatic illustration is shown in 
Fig. 1. 

5.3 Classification — Goat and sheep skins are 
classified on the basis of the length of the back- 
bone line as shown in Table 2.
